::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- chain operations with the native pipe `|>` and read a pipeline aloud;
- keep rows with `filter()` and choose columns with `select()` and its helpers;
- create and recode variables with `mutate()`, `if_else()` and `case_when()`;
- sort rows with `arrange()` and `desc()`, and relate them to base R `order()`;
- tidy up a table with `rename()`, `relocate()`, `distinct()`, `slice_*()` and `count()`.
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
```
:::


## 1. Why a "grammar" of data manipulation?

Most of the time spent on a real analysis is not spent on statistics: it is spent getting the data into shape. *Keep only the adult patients. Convert grams to kilograms. Sort by date. Count how many observations per group.*

Base R can do all of this with brackets, but the code quickly becomes hard to read. The **dplyr** package gives each of these tasks a **verb** — a function with a clear name — and all verbs work the same way:

1. the first argument is a data frame;
2. the other arguments describe what to do, using column names **without quotes**;
3. the result is a new data frame (the original is never modified).

We will use `penguins` throughout. Converting it to a tibble once keeps the printed output short:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins <- as_tibble(penguins)
penguins
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 344 × 8
#>    species island    bill_len bill_dep flipper_len body_mass sex     year
#>    <fct>   <fct>        <dbl>    <dbl>       <int>     <int> <fct>  <int>
#>  1 Adelie  Torgersen     39.1     18.7         181      3750 male    2007
#>  2 Adelie  Torgersen     39.5     17.4         186      3800 female  2007
#>  3 Adelie  Torgersen     40.3     18           195      3250 female  2007
#>  4 Adelie  Torgersen     NA       NA            NA        NA <NA>    2007
#>  5 Adelie  Torgersen     36.7     19.3         193      3450 female  2007
#>  6 Adelie  Torgersen     39.3     20.6         190      3650 male    2007
#>  7 Adelie  Torgersen     38.9     17.8         181      3625 female  2007
#>  8 Adelie  Torgersen     39.2     19.6         195      4675 male    2007
#>  9 Adelie  Torgersen     34.1     18.1         193      3475 <NA>    2007
#> 10 Adelie  Torgersen     42       20.2         190      4250 <NA>    2007
#> # ℹ 334 more rows
```


:::
:::


## 2. The pipe `|>`: "and then"

Suppose we want the Gentoo penguins, then only three columns, then sorted by mass. Without a pipe, we either nest the calls (read from the inside out) or create intermediate objects:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
arrange(select(filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo"),
               species, sex, body_mass), body_mass)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 124 × 3
#>    species sex    body_mass
#>    <fct>   <fct>      <int>
#>  1 Gentoo  female      3950
#>  2 Gentoo  <NA>        4100
#>  3 Gentoo  female      4150
#>  4 Gentoo  female      4200
#>  5 Gentoo  female      4200
#>  6 Gentoo  female      4200
#>  7 Gentoo  female      4300
#>  8 Gentoo  female      4300
#>  9 Gentoo  female      4350
#> 10 Gentoo  female      4375
#> # ℹ 114 more rows
```


:::
:::


The **pipe** `|>` takes what is on its left and passes it as the **first argument** of the function on its right. `x |> f(y)` is the same as `f(x, y)`. Read it aloud as **"and then"**:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>                              # take penguins, and then
  filter(species == "Gentoo") |>         # keep the Gentoo, and then
  select(species, sex, body_mass) |>     # keep three columns, and then
  arrange(body_mass)                     # sort by body mass
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 124 × 3
#>    species sex    body_mass
#>    <fct>   <fct>      <int>
#>  1 Gentoo  female      3950
#>  2 Gentoo  <NA>        4100
#>  3 Gentoo  female      4150
#>  4 Gentoo  female      4200
#>  5 Gentoo  female      4200
#>  6 Gentoo  female      4200
#>  7 Gentoo  female      4300
#>  8 Gentoo  female      4300
#>  9 Gentoo  female      4350
#> 10 Gentoo  female      4375
#> # ℹ 114 more rows
```


:::
:::


The two chunks produce the same result, but the second one reads in the order in which things happen. Put one verb per line, with `|>` at the end of each line.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: `|>` vs `%>%`

The native pipe `|>` has been part of R since version 4.1. Older code (and many web pages) use `%>%` from the magrittr package, which behaves almost identically for everyday use. In this course we always use `|>`. The keyboard shortcut in RStudio and Positron is Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + M (tick "Use native pipe operator" in the options).
:::

## 3. `filter()`: keep rows

`filter()` keeps the rows for which a condition is `TRUE`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie", island == "Dream", flipper_len > 190)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 22 × 8
#>    species island bill_len bill_dep flipper_len body_mass sex     year
#>    <fct>   <fct>     <dbl>    <dbl>       <int>     <int> <fct>  <int>
#>  1 Adelie  Dream      36.4     17           195      3325 female  2007
#>  2 Adelie  Dream      39.2     21.1         196      4150 male    2007
#>  3 Adelie  Dream      40.8     18.4         195      3900 male    2007
#>  4 Adelie  Dream      44.1     19.7         196      4400 male    2007
#>  5 Adelie  Dream      42.3     21.2         191      4150 male    2007
#>  6 Adelie  Dream      37.3     17.8         191      3350 female  2008
#>  7 Adelie  Dream      41.3     20.3         194      3550 male    2008
#>  8 Adelie  Dream      35.7     18           202      3550 female  2008
#>  9 Adelie  Dream      41.1     18.1         205      4300 male    2008
#> 10 Adelie  Dream      40.8     18.9         208      4300 male    2008
#> # ℹ 12 more rows
```


:::
:::


Conditions separated by commas must **all** be true (logical "and"). For "or" use `|`. The comparison operators are the ones you met with [vectors](../01-foundations/04-vectors.qmd): `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`.

Three helpers make conditions shorter and clearer:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Value in a set: %in%
penguins |> filter(species %in% c("Adelie", "Chinstrap")) |> nrow()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 220
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Value in a range (both ends included): between()
penguins |> filter(between(body_mass, 3500, 4000)) |> nrow()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 99
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Missing values: is.na()
penguins |> filter(is.na(sex))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 11 × 8
#>    species island    bill_len bill_dep flipper_len body_mass sex    year
#>    <fct>   <fct>        <dbl>    <dbl>       <int>     <int> <fct> <int>
#>  1 Adelie  Torgersen     NA       NA            NA        NA <NA>   2007
#>  2 Adelie  Torgersen     34.1     18.1         193      3475 <NA>   2007
#>  3 Adelie  Torgersen     42       20.2         190      4250 <NA>   2007
#>  4 Adelie  Torgersen     37.8     17.1         186      3300 <NA>   2007
#>  5 Adelie  Torgersen     37.8     17.3         180      3700 <NA>   2007
#>  6 Adelie  Dream         37.5     18.9         179      2975 <NA>   2007
#>  7 Gentoo  Biscoe        44.5     14.3         216      4100 <NA>   2007
#>  8 Gentoo  Biscoe        46.2     14.4         214      4650 <NA>   2008
#>  9 Gentoo  Biscoe        47.3     13.8         216      4725 <NA>   2009
#> 10 Gentoo  Biscoe        44.5     15.7         217      4875 <NA>   2009
#> 11 Gentoo  Biscoe        NA       NA            NA        NA <NA>   2009
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- `%in%` is cleaner than `species == "Adelie" | species == "Chinstrap"`.
- `between(x, 3500, 4000)` means `x >= 3500 & x <= 4000`.
- The last table shows the 11 penguins whose sex was not recorded. `filter(!is.na(sex))` keeps the others.
- `filter()` **drops rows where the condition is `NA`**, so penguins with missing `body_mass` are silently excluded from the `between()` count.
:::

## 4. `select()`: choose columns


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |> select(species, island, body_mass)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 344 × 3
#>    species island    body_mass
#>    <fct>   <fct>         <int>
#>  1 Adelie  Torgersen      3750
#>  2 Adelie  Torgersen      3800
#>  3 Adelie  Torgersen      3250
#>  4 Adelie  Torgersen        NA
#>  5 Adelie  Torgersen      3450
#>  6 Adelie  Torgersen      3650
#>  7 Adelie  Torgersen      3625
#>  8 Adelie  Torgersen      4675
#>  9 Adelie  Torgersen      3475
#> 10 Adelie  Torgersen      4250
#> # ℹ 334 more rows
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |> select(-year, -island)        # everything except
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 344 × 6
#>    species bill_len bill_dep flipper_len body_mass sex   
#>    <fct>      <dbl>    <dbl>       <int>     <int> <fct> 
#>  1 Adelie      39.1     18.7         181      3750 male  
#>  2 Adelie      39.5     17.4         186      3800 female
#>  3 Adelie      40.3     18           195      3250 female
#>  4 Adelie      NA       NA            NA        NA <NA>  
#>  5 Adelie      36.7     19.3         193      3450 female
#>  6 Adelie      39.3     20.6         190      3650 male  
#>  7 Adelie      38.9     17.8         181      3625 female
#>  8 Adelie      39.2     19.6         195      4675 male  
#>  9 Adelie      34.1     18.1         193      3475 <NA>  
#> 10 Adelie      42       20.2         190      4250 <NA>  
#> # ℹ 334 more rows
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |> select(species:bill_dep)      # a range of columns
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 344 × 4
#>    species island    bill_len bill_dep
#>    <fct>   <fct>        <dbl>    <dbl>
#>  1 Adelie  Torgersen     39.1     18.7
#>  2 Adelie  Torgersen     39.5     17.4
#>  3 Adelie  Torgersen     40.3     18  
#>  4 Adelie  Torgersen     NA       NA  
#>  5 Adelie  Torgersen     36.7     19.3
#>  6 Adelie  Torgersen     39.3     20.6
#>  7 Adelie  Torgersen     38.9     17.8
#>  8 Adelie  Torgersen     39.2     19.6
#>  9 Adelie  Torgersen     34.1     18.1
#> 10 Adelie  Torgersen     42       20.2
#> # ℹ 334 more rows
```


:::
:::


**Selection helpers** pick columns by their name or type:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |> select(species, starts_with("bill"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 344 × 3
#>    species bill_len bill_dep
#>    <fct>      <dbl>    <dbl>
#>  1 Adelie      39.1     18.7
#>  2 Adelie      39.5     17.4
#>  3 Adelie      40.3     18  
#>  4 Adelie      NA       NA  
#>  5 Adelie      36.7     19.3
#>  6 Adelie      39.3     20.6
#>  7 Adelie      38.9     17.8
#>  8 Adelie      39.2     19.6
#>  9 Adelie      34.1     18.1
#> 10 Adelie      42       20.2
#> # ℹ 334 more rows
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |> select(where(is.numeric))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 344 × 5
#>    bill_len bill_dep flipper_len body_mass  year
#>       <dbl>    <dbl>       <int>     <int> <int>
#>  1     39.1     18.7         181      3750  2007
#>  2     39.5     17.4         186      3800  2007
#>  3     40.3     18           195      3250  2007
#>  4     NA       NA            NA        NA  2007
#>  5     36.7     19.3         193      3450  2007
#>  6     39.3     20.6         190      3650  2007
#>  7     38.9     17.8         181      3625  2007
#>  8     39.2     19.6         195      4675  2007
#>  9     34.1     18.1         193      3475  2007
#> 10     42       20.2         190      4250  2007
#> # ℹ 334 more rows
```


:::
:::


Other helpers: `ends_with()`, `contains()`, `everything()`, `all_of(vec)` (names stored in a character vector). `where()` takes a function that returns `TRUE`/`FALSE` for each column: `where(is.factor)`, `where(is.numeric)`.

## 5. `mutate()`: create or modify columns

`mutate()` adds new columns computed from existing ones (or overwrites them, if you reuse a name).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  mutate(
    body_mass_kg = body_mass / 1000,
    bill_ratio   = bill_len / bill_dep
  ) |>
  select(species, body_mass_kg, bill_ratio)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 344 × 3
#>    species body_mass_kg bill_ratio
#>    <fct>          <dbl>      <dbl>
#>  1 Adelie         3.75       2.091
#>  2 Adelie         3.8        2.270
#>  3 Adelie         3.25       2.239
#>  4 Adelie        NA         NA    
#>  5 Adelie         3.45       1.902
#>  6 Adelie         3.65       1.908
#>  7 Adelie         3.625      2.185
#>  8 Adelie         4.675      2    
#>  9 Adelie         3.475      1.884
#> 10 Adelie         4.25       2.079
#> # ℹ 334 more rows
```


:::
:::


Columns created earlier in the same `mutate()` can be used immediately afterwards.

### Two-way recoding: `if_else()`


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  mutate(heavy = if_else(body_mass > 4500, "heavy", "light")) |>
  count(heavy)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   heavy     n
#>   <chr> <int>
#> 1 heavy   115
#> 2 light   227
#> 3 <NA>      2
```


:::
:::


`if_else(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false)`. Where the condition is `NA`, the result is `NA` — which is honest: we do not know whether a penguin with unknown mass is heavy.

### Many categories: `case_when()`


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  mutate(
    size = case_when(
      body_mass < 3500 ~ "small",
      body_mass < 4500 ~ "medium",
      body_mass >= 4500 ~ "large",
      .default = NA
    )
  ) |>
  count(size)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   size       n
#>   <chr>  <int>
#> 1 large    118
#> 2 medium   153
#> 3 small     71
#> 4 <NA>       2
```


:::
:::


Each line is `condition ~ value`. Conditions are checked **in order**, and the first one that is true wins: a penguin of 3000 g matches the first line and never reaches the second. `.default` gives the value when no condition is true.

Turning a numeric variable into classes like this is called **discretisation**. It is handy for tables, but it throws information away: for statistical models, keep the original number whenever you can.

## 6. `arrange()`: sort rows

### Base R first: `sort()` and `order()`


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- c(5, 1, 10)
sort(x)        # the sorted values
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1]  1  5 10
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
order(x)       # the positions that would sort x
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 2 1 3
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
x[order(x)]    # using those positions
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1]  1  5 10
```


:::
:::


To sort a data frame in base R we put `order()` in the row position:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
head(penguins[order(penguins$body_mass), c("species", "body_mass")], 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   species   body_mass
#>   <fct>         <int>
#> 1 Chinstrap      2700
#> 2 Adelie         2850
#> 3 Adelie         2850
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# descending: put a minus in front (numeric columns only)
head(penguins[order(-penguins$body_mass), c("species", "body_mass")], 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   species body_mass
#>   <fct>       <int>
#> 1 Gentoo       6300
#> 2 Gentoo       6050
#> 3 Gentoo       6000
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# by species, then by decreasing bill length
head(penguins[order(penguins$species, -penguins$bill_len),
              c("species", "bill_len")], 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   species bill_len
#>   <fct>      <dbl>
#> 1 Adelie      46  
#> 2 Adelie      45.8
#> 3 Adelie      45.6
```


:::
:::


### The dplyr way


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |> arrange(body_mass)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

#>    species   island    bill_len bill_dep flipper_len body_mass sex     year
#>    <fct>     <fct>        <dbl>    <dbl>       <int>     <int> <fct>  <int>
#>  1 Chinstrap Dream         46.9     16.6         192      2700 female  2008
#>  2 Adelie    Biscoe        36.5     16.6         181      2850 female  2008
#>  3 Adelie    Biscoe        36.4     17.1         184      2850 female  2008
#>  4 Adelie    Biscoe        34.5     18.1         187      2900 female  2008
#>  5 Adelie    Dream         33.1     16.1         178      2900 female  2008

#> 10 Adelie    Dream         37       16.9         185      3000 female  2007
#> # ℹ 334 more rows
```

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |> arrange(desc(body_mass))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

#>  2 Adelie  Torgersen     45.8     18.9         197      4150 male   2008

#> 10 Adelie  Torgersen     42.8     18.5         195      4250 male   2008
#> # ℹ 334 more rows
```


:::
:::


`desc()` works for any type (numbers, text, factors), while the minus trick only works for numbers. With several columns, ties in the first are broken by the second. In both approaches, **missing values go last**.

## 7. Small but useful verbs


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  rename(mass_g = body_mass, flipper_mm = flipper_len) |>   # new = old
  relocate(year, .before = species)                         # move a column
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}


`distinct()` keeps unique rows (or unique combinations of the columns you name):


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |> distinct(species, island)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
```

The `slice_*()` family selects rows by **position**:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |> slice_head(n = 3)                    # first 3 rows
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 3 × 8
#>   species island    bill_len bill_dep flipper_len body_mass sex     year
#>   <fct>   <fct>        <dbl>    <dbl>       <int>     <int> <fct>  <int>

#> 2 Adelie  Torgersen     39.5     17.4         186      3800 female  2007
#> 3 Adelie  Torgersen     40.3     18           195      3250 female  2007
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |> slice_max(body_mass, n = 3)          # 3 heaviest
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 4 × 8
#>   species island bill_len bill_dep flipper_len body_mass sex    year
#>   <fct>   <fct>     <dbl>    <dbl>       <int>     <int> <fct> <int>

#> 2 Gentoo  Biscoe     59.6     17           230      6050 male   2007
#> 3 Gentoo  Biscoe     51.1     16.3         220      6000 male   2008
#> 4 Gentoo  Biscoe     48.8     16.2         222      6000 male   2009
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |> slice_min(bill_len, n = 1, by = species)   # shortest bill per species
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

#>   species   island bill_len bill_dep flipper_len body_mass sex     year
#>   <fct>     <fct>     <dbl>    <dbl>       <int>     <int> <fct>  <int>
#> 1 Adelie    Dream      32.1     15.5         188      3050 female  2009
#> 2 Gentoo    Biscoe     40.9     13.7         214      4650 female  2007
#> 3 Chinstrap Dream      40.9     16.6         187      3200 female  2008
```


:::
:::


`slice_max()` keeps **ties**: if several penguins share the third-highest mass, they are all returned (use `with_ties = FALSE` to get exactly `n` rows). The argument `by =` repeats the operation within each group — more on groups in the [next lesson](10-grouped-summaries.qmd). For random rows, use `slice_sample(n = 5)` (after `set.seed()`).

`count()` counts the rows for each combination of values:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |> count(species)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   species       n
#>   <fct>     <int>
#> 1 Adelie      152
#> 2 Chinstrap    68
#> 3 Gentoo      124
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |> count(species, sex, sort = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>   species   sex        n
#>   <fct>     <fct>  <int>
#> 1 Adelie    female    73
#> 2 Adelie    male      73
#> 3 Gentoo    male      61
#> 4 Gentoo    female    58
#> 5 Chinstrap female    34
#> 6 Chinstrap male      34
#> 7 Adelie    <NA>       6
#> 8 Gentoo    <NA>       5
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

Each row of a `count()` result is one combination of the grouping variables, and `n` is the number of units with that combination. These are **absolute frequencies**; you will turn them into proportions and contingency tables in [Frequency tables](../05-descriptive/21-frequency-tables.qmd). Note the `NA` rows for sex: `count()` does not hide missing values, which is exactly what you want when checking data.
:::

## 8. Putting it together

A typical pipeline answers a question from start to finish. *Among penguins with known sex, which five have the largest bill-to-depth ratio, and on which island do they live?*


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  mutate(bill_ratio = bill_len / bill_dep) |>
  select(species, island, sex, bill_ratio) |>
  arrange(desc(bill_ratio)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   species island sex    bill_ratio
#>   <fct>   <fct>  <fct>       <dbl>
#> 1 Gentoo  Biscoe male        3.613
#> 2 Gentoo  Biscoe male        3.510
#> 3 Gentoo  Biscoe male        3.506
#> 4 Gentoo  Biscoe female      3.492
#> 5 Gentoo  Biscoe male        3.459
```


:::
:::


Notice that nothing has been saved: `penguins` is unchanged. To keep a result, assign it: `result <- penguins |> ...`.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **`=` instead of `==` in `filter()`.** `filter(species = "Adelie")` gives an error; comparison needs `==`.
2. **`species == "Adelie" | "Gentoo"`** does not mean what it seems. Write `species %in% c("Adelie", "Gentoo")`.
3. **Forgetting to assign.** A pipeline only prints its result; `penguins` is not modified unless you write `penguins <- penguins |> ...`.
4. **Quoting column names** in dplyr verbs (`select("species")` works, but `filter("body_mass" > 4000)` compares two constants!). Use bare names.
5. **Expecting exactly `n` rows from `slice_max()`.** Ties are kept by default.
6. **Order matters in `case_when()`.** Put the most specific conditions first.
:::

## 9. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. Read this pipeline aloud: `penguins |> filter(year == 2009) |> count(island)`.

"Take penguins, **and then** keep the rows from 2009, **and then** count the rows for each island." The result has one row per island with the number of penguins measured in 2009.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. What is the difference between `select()` and `filter()`?

`filter()` works on **rows** (units), keeping those that satisfy a condition. `select()` works on **columns** (variables), keeping the ones you name. The number of rows changes with `filter()`; the number of columns changes with `select()`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. A penguin has `body_mass = NA`. What does `if_else(body_mass > 4500, "heavy", "light")` return for it?

`NA`. The condition `NA > 4500` is unknown, so the result is unknown. If you want a separate label, use `case_when(is.na(body_mass) ~ "unknown", body_mass > 4500 ~ "heavy", .default = "light")`.
:::

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — base R vs dplyr.** With `mtcars`, list the three cars with the highest `mpg` among those with 4 cylinders, showing only `mpg`, `cyl` and `hp`. Do it twice: once with `order()` and brackets, once with dplyr (keep the car names with `rownames_to_column()`).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
# base R
cars4 <- mtcars[mtcars$cyl == 4, c("mpg", "cyl", "hp")]
head(cars4[order(-cars4$mpg), ], 3)

# dplyr
mtcars |>
  rownames_to_column("model") |>
  filter(cyl == 4) |>
  select(model, mpg, cyl, hp) |>
  arrange(desc(mpg)) |>
  slice_head(n = 3)
```
Both give the Toyota Corolla, Fiat 128 and Honda Civic. The dplyr version is longer but each line does one thing.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Verb | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `filter()` | keep rows | `filter(x > 0, g %in% c("a", "b"))` |
| `select()` | choose columns | `select(a, starts_with("b"), where(is.numeric))` |
| `mutate()` | create / modify columns | `mutate(z = x / y)` |
| `if_else()`, `case_when()` | recode | `case_when(x < 0 ~ "neg", .default = "pos")` |
| `arrange()`, `desc()` | sort rows | `arrange(g, desc(x))` |
| `order()` (base) | sorting positions | `df[order(-df$x), ]` |
| `rename()`, `relocate()` | rename / move columns | `rename(new = old)` |
| `distinct()` | unique rows | `distinct(g1, g2)` |
| `slice_head()`, `slice_max()`, `slice_sample()` | rows by position | `slice_max(x, n = 3)` |
| `count()` | frequencies | `count(g, sort = TRUE)` |

- Every verb takes a data frame and returns a new one; nothing is modified in place.
- The pipe `|>` passes the result on its left as the first argument of the function on its right: read it as "and then", and write one verb per line.
- `filter()` drops rows whose condition is `NA`; check missing values with `filter(is.na(x))` or `count()`.
